lists.title: Latin A1 Grammar Path
lists.description: First Latin: the nominative/accusative case pair, the first and second declensions, the irregular verb sum, first-conjugation present tense, adjective agreement, the two-way preposition in, and why word order is flexible.

lists.title: Latin A2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Growing Latin: the imperfect and future tenses, the third declension with its neuters, personal pronouns and demonstratives, the third and fourth conjugations, commands, questions, and the genitive and dative at work.

lists.title: Latin B1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Real reading: the perfect and pluperfect, the fourth and fifth declensions, adjective comparison and adverbs, the present passive, the perfect participle, and relative clauses with qui.

lists.title: Latin B2 Grammar Path
lists.description: The subjunctive age: its present and imperfect forms, purpose and result clauses, cum-clauses, the accusative-and-infinitive, the ablative absolute, and deponent verbs.

lists.title: Latin C1 Grammar Path
lists.description: Command of the machine: gerund and gerundive with the passive periphrastic, indirect questions under the sequence of tenses, and the three conditional types.

lists.title: Latin C2 Grammar Path
lists.description: Mastery: sustained oratio obliqua, poetic word order on real classical lines, and register from the Ciceronian period to the colloquial letter.

points.title: Nominative and accusative: subject and direct object
points.function: Tell who does the action from who or what receives it
points.explanation: Latin marks a noun's job in the sentence with its ENDING, not its position. The subject (who's doing it) takes the nominative case; the direct object (what's acted on) takes the accusative. Puella becomes puellam when it's the object: Puella puerum amat ("The girl loves the boy") vs. Puer puellam amat ("The boy loves the girl") — swap the endings and the meaning flips, even if you also swap the word order.

drills.translation: The girl sees the boy.
The master has water.
The boy loves the island.

points.title: First declension nouns: -a / -ae feminine
points.function: Recognize and form the most common noun pattern
points.explanation: Most first-declension nouns are feminine and end -a in the nominative singular (puella, aqua, terra, insula). The genitive singular ends -ae, which gives the whole declension its name and means "of the ___": puellae = "of the girl" / "the girl's." The accusative singular ends -am: puella → puellam.

drills.translation: The girl lives on the island.
The girl's name is Julia.
I have water and land.

points.title: Second declension nouns: -us masculine and -um neuter
points.function: Learn the other core noun pattern
points.explanation: Second-declension nouns end -us (masculine, like dominus) or -um (neuter, like bellum) in the nominative. Neuter nouns are special: their nominative and accusative forms are IDENTICAL — bellum stays bellum whether it's the subject or the object. Only masculine and feminine nouns change shape between the two.

drills.translation: The war is great.
drills.hint: war — neuter, same form for subject or object

drills.translation: The boy sees the war.
drills.hint: war — neuter object looks just like the subject form

drills.translation: The master is good.

points.title: sum, esse — the irregular verb "to be"
points.function: Say what something or someone IS
points.explanation: Sum ("I am") is Latin's most irregular verb, just as "to be" is irregular in English: sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt. Sum takes no direct object — instead of an accusative, it links right back to the nominative: Puella bona est ("The girl is good"), not puellam.

drills.translation: The girl is good.
We are good.
drills.hint: we are — 1st person plural of sum

drills.translation: You are good.
drills.hint: you are — 2nd person singular of sum

points.title: First conjugation present tense (-are verbs)
points.function: Conjugate the largest family of Latin verbs
points.explanation: Verbs like amo ("I love") belong to the first conjugation, spotted by the -are infinitive (amare). The present tense endings are -o, -as, -at, -amus, -atis, -ant, added to the stem ama-: amo, amas, amat, amamus, amatis, amant. Because the ending already shows the person, Latin usually drops the pronoun.

drills.translation: The girl loves the boy.
I love the island.
drills.hint: I love — 1st person singular, no pronoun needed

drills.translation: We love the land.

points.title: Adjective-noun agreement
points.function: Match adjective endings to the noun they describe
points.explanation: Latin adjectives change their ending to match the noun's gender, number, and case: magnus (masculine), magna (feminine), and magnum (neuter) all mean "big." Puella magna and dominus magnus both mean "big," but the ending has to match the Latin noun, not the English word.

drills.translation: The girl is big.
The master is big.
The war is big.

points.title: Prepositions: in + accusative vs. in + ablative
points.function: Choose the right case after "in"
points.explanation: The preposition in changes meaning with the case that follows it: in + accusative means motion INTO (in insulam = "into the island"), while in + ablative means location IN or ON (in insula = "on the island"). Same preposition, different case, different meaning — a pattern Latin uses with several two-way prepositions.

drills.translation: The girl lives on the island.
The boy comes onto the island.
The water is on the land.

points.title: Word order: Latin puts case marking to work
points.function: Understand why word order is flexible in Latin
points.explanation: Because endings — not position — show who does what, Latin word order is flexible for emphasis, though the neutral default is Subject-Object-Verb: Puella puerum amat, literally "girl boy loves." Puerum puella amat and Amat puella puerum mean the same thing; only the endings, never the order, decide who loves whom.

drills.translation: The girl loves the boy. (default subject-object-verb order)
drills.hint: loves — verb comes last in the neutral order

drills.translation: The girl loves the boy. (verb fronted for emphasis)
drills.hint: loves — same verb, moved to the front

drills.translation: The girl loves the boy. (object fronted)
drills.hint: girl — the subject can move without changing meaning, thanks to its ending

points.title: Second conjugation present tense (-ere verbs with -e-)
points.function: Conjugate the video/habeo family in the present

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: Verbs like video ("I see") and habeo ("I have") belong to the second conjugation, spotted by the long -e- of the infinitive: videre, habere. The present endings are the familiar -o, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt, but the -e- of the stem stays visible everywhere: video, vides, videt, videmus, videtis, vident. Compare first-conjugation amas/amat with second-conjugation vides/videt — the vowel before the ending tells you which family you are in.

drills.translation: The boy sees the girl.
I have water.
We see the island.
The girls see the master.
You see the land.

points.title: possum, posse — "to be able" with an infinitive
points.function: Say what someone can or cannot do

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: Possum ("I am able, I can") is sum wearing a prefix: pot- + sum gives possum, potes, potest, possumus, potestis, possunt (t + s fuses to ss). Like English "can," it takes an infinitive to name the action: Puella videre potest ("The girl is able to see"). Add non before it to say what someone cannot do: non possum ("I cannot").

drills.translation: The girl can see the water.
drills.hint: can — 3rd person singular of the 'be able' verb

drills.translation: I can see the island.
We can see the war.
You can love the boy.
The boys can have water.

points.title: Imperfect tense (-bam): what used to happen
points.function: Describe ongoing or repeated action in the past

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The imperfect paints the past as ongoing, repeated, or background: amabam means "I was loving, I used to love." Its signature is -ba-: amabam, amabas, amabat, amabamus, amabatis, amabant, and the same -ba- works in every conjugation (videbam, habebat). Sum has its own imperfect: eram, eras, erat, eramus, eratis, erant.

drills.translation: The girl once loved the boy.
I once had water.
drills.hint: I used to have — imperfect 1st singular

drills.translation: We used to live on the island.
The master was good.
The boys were watching the war.

points.title: Future tense (-bo/-bis and -am/-es)
points.function: Say what will happen

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: First and second conjugations build the future with -b-: amabo, amabis, amabit, amabimus, amabitis, amabunt ("I will love, you will love..."), and likewise videbo, habebis. Third and fourth conjugations use a different set, -am, -es, -et: dicam, dices, dicet. Sum again goes its own way: ero, eris, erit, erimus, eritis, erunt.

drills.translation: The girl will love the boy tomorrow.
Tomorrow I will have water.
We will soon see the island.
The war will be great.
drills.hint: will be — the future of sum

drills.translation: You will live on the land.

points.title: Third declension nouns: rex, regis and urbs, urbis
points.function: Handle the biggest and most varied noun family

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin declension
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: Third-declension nouns have unpredictable nominatives (rex "king," urbs "city," miles "soldier") but reliable endings on the stem you get from the genitive: reg-is, urb-is, milit-is. Learn every third-declension noun as a pair — rex, regis. The core singular endings are accusative -em (regem), genitive -is (regis), dative -i (regi), ablative -e (rege).

drills.translation: The king lives in the city.
The girl sees the king in the city.
The king loves the city.
The name of the city is Rome.
We live in the city.

points.title: Third declension neuters: corpus, tempus, nomen
points.function: Spot the neuters whose subject and object forms match

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin declension
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: Third-declension neuters like corpus ("body"), tempus ("time"), and nomen ("name") follow the universal neuter law: nominative and accusative are identical, in both numbers. Their stems appear in the genitive — corporis, temporis, nominis — and the nominative/accusative plural ends in -a: corpora, tempora, nomina. Do not let corpus and tempus fool you: the -us is not the second declension's -us.

drills.translation: The boy's body is big.
The boy has time.
drills.hint: time — neuter; the object looks like the subject form

drills.translation: The boy's name is Marcus.
The bodies are big.
The king has a new name.
drills.hint: name — neuter accusative, same as the subject form

points.title: Personal pronouns: ego, tu, nos, vos
points.function: Use I/you/we pronouns for emphasis and as objects

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin grammar
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: Because verb endings already show the person, the nominative pronouns ego ("I"), tu ("you"), nos ("we"), vos ("you all") appear mainly for emphasis or contrast: Ego amo ("I love — I, not you"). Their object forms are me, te, nos, vos (accusative), and the datives are mihi, tibi, nobis, vobis ("to me, to you..."). Nos and vos look the same as subject and object — context and the verb decide.

drills.translation: I love the girl. (emphatic)
The girl loves me.
drills.hint: the object form of the first person

drills.translation: We see you.
I love you.
You all see us.
drills.hint: us — object form, identical to the subject form

points.title: Demonstratives: hic "this" and ille "that"
points.function: Point at things near and far

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin declension
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: Hic, haec, hoc means "this (near me)"; ille, illa, illud means "that (over there)" — and ille is the ancestor of the Romance articles. Both agree with their noun in gender, number, and case: hic puer, haec puella, hoc bellum; accusatives hunc, hanc, hoc and illum, illam, illud. They also stand alone as pronouns: ille = "that man, he."

drills.translation: This girl is good.
That master is bad.
The boy loves that girl.
This war is great.
The king sees this city.

points.title: Third and fourth conjugation present (dico, audio)
points.function: Complete the present tense across all four conjugations

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The third conjugation (dico "I say," mitto, duco; infinitive -ere with short e) runs dico, dicis, dicit, dicimus, dicitis, dicunt — a short, changeable vowel where the first two conjugations keep a steady -a- or -e-. The fourth conjugation (audio "I hear," venio; infinitive -ire) keeps its -i-: audio, audis, audit, audimus, auditis, audiunt. Note the 3rd plural: dicunt but audiunt.

drills.translation: The girl says a word.
I hear the king in the city.
The boys hear the master.
We say words.
You hear the girl.

points.title: Imperatives: giving commands
points.function: Tell someone to do something

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The singular imperative is usually the bare present stem: ama! ("love!"), vide!, audi!; the plural adds -te: amate!, videte!, audite! Third-conjugation verbs use -e / -ite: mitte!, mittite! Four irregulars drop the vowel in the singular — dic! ("say!"), duc! ("lead!"), fac! ("do!"), fer! ("carry!"). The person commanded often appears in the vocative: Porta aquam, puer!

drills.translation: Carry the water, boy!
Listen to the king, boys!
Tell me the word!
See the girl, master!
drills.hint: see! — singular command of the 2nd conjugation

drills.translation: Come onto the island, girls!

points.title: Questions: -ne, quis and quid
points.function: Ask yes/no and who/what questions

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin grammar
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: A yes/no question hangs the little particle -ne on the first word, usually the verb: Videsne puellam? ("Do you see the girl?"). Question words do the rest: quis? ("who?"), quid? ("what?") — Quis aquam habet? ("Who has the water?"). Latin has no word for "do" in questions; the particle or the question word alone does the job.

drills.translation: Do you see the girl?
drills.hint: do you see? — verb + the question particle

drills.translation: Who has the water?
What is the boy saying?
Is the master good?
drills.hint: is...? — the verb 'to be' with the question particle attached

drills.translation: Does the girl love the boy?
drills.hint: does she love? — verb first with -ne attached

points.title: Genitive and dative at work
points.function: Say whose something is and to whom it goes

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin declension
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The genitive answers "whose? of what?": filius regis ("the king's son, the son of the king"). The dative marks the indirect object — the person to or for whom something is done: Puer puellae aquam dat ("The boy gives water to the girl"). First declension: genitive and dative singular both -ae; second declension: genitive -i, dative -o; third declension: genitive -is, dative -i.

drills.translation: The boy gives water to the girl.
The king's son is good.
The master gives land to the boy.
The water of the island is good.
The king speaks words to the people.

points.title: Perfect tense: amavi, vidi, dixi
points.function: Report completed past actions

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The perfect states that something happened and is done: amavit — "she loved, she has loved." It is built on the perfect stem, the third principal part you memorize with each verb: amo/amavi, video/vidi, dico/dixi, venio/veni. The endings are the same for every verb: -i, -isti, -it, -imus, -istis, -erunt. Sum's perfect is fui.

drills.translation: The queen loved the king.
Yesterday I saw the king.
We said good words.
The boys came onto the island.
You have always been good.
drills.hint: you have been — perfect of sum

points.title: Pluperfect tense: amaveram "I had loved"
points.function: Reach further back — past before the past

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The pluperfect says an action was already complete before another past moment: amaveram — "I had loved." The recipe is simple: perfect stem + the imperfect of sum as endings: amaveram, amaveras, amaverat, amaveramus, amaveratis, amaverant; likewise videram ("I had seen") and dixerat ("he had said").

drills.translation: The girl had loved the boy for a long time.
I had seen the city before.
The king had said the words.
We had come into the city.
The boys had had water.

points.title: Fourth and fifth declension: manus and dies
points.function: Finish the noun system with the -us and -es families

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin declension
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The fourth declension runs on -u-: manus ("hand," feminine), manus, manui, manum, manu — its nominative and genitive singular look identical. The fifth runs on -e-: dies ("day," usually masculine) and res ("thing, matter"): dies, diei, diem, die. These two families are small but their members are everywhere — manus, domus, dies, res, spes.

drills.translation: The day is long.
The boy sees the girl's hand.
drills.hint: hand — accusative of the fourth declension

drills.translation: The matter is great.
I was in the city for many days.
drills.hint: days — accusative of duration, looks like the nominative

drills.translation: The boy has water in his hand.

points.title: Comparison of adjectives: altior, altissimus
points.function: Say taller, tallest, very tall

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin declension
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The comparative adds -ior (neuter -ius) to the stem: altior ("taller, rather tall"), longius. The superlative adds -issimus, -a, -um: altissimus ("tallest, very tall"), fortissimus. To compare two things, use quam ("than"): Puella altior quam puer est ("The girl is taller than the boy") — or put the second item in the ablative with no quam at all.

drills.translation: This boy is taller.
This war is longer.
The king is very brave.
The girl is taller than the boy.
This road is very long.

points.title: Adverbs: bene, fortiter, celeriter
points.function: Describe how an action is done

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin grammar
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: First/second-declension adjectives make adverbs in -e: longe ("far") from longus; third-declension adjectives use -iter: fortiter ("bravely") from fortis, celeriter ("quickly") from celer. A few of the commonest are irregular: bene ("well") from bonus, male ("badly") from malus. Adverbs never change form — no agreement to worry about.

drills.translation: The girl sings well.
The soldiers fight bravely.
The boy speaks badly.
The girl lives far away.
The boy runs quickly.

points.title: Present passive: amatur "is loved"
points.function: Flip the sentence — the subject receives the action

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The passive swaps the endings: -or, -ris, -tur, -mur, -mini, -ntur. Amat ("she loves") becomes amatur ("she is loved"); vident becomes videntur. The doer, if named, goes in the ablative with a/ab: Puella a puero amatur ("The girl is loved by the boy") — ab before vowels.

drills.translation: The girl is loved by the boy.
The city is seen by the king.
The words are heard by the girls.
The water is carried by the master.
We are seen by the king.

points.title: Perfect passive participle and perfect passive
points.function: Say what was done with participle + est

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The fourth principal part gives the perfect passive participle: amatus, -a, -um ("loved"), visus ("seen"), captus ("captured"), portatus ("carried"). With the present of sum it builds the perfect passive: Urbs capta est ("The city was captured"). The participle agrees with the subject like any adjective — puella amata est, verba audita sunt.

drills.translation: The girl was loved by the boy.
drills.hint: loved — participle agreeing with a feminine subject

drills.translation: The city was captured.
The words were heard.
The boy was seen by the master.
The water was carried by the boy.

points.title: Relative clauses: qui, quae, quod
points.function: Attach a whole clause to a noun

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The relative pronoun qui, quae, quod ("who, which") takes its gender and number from the noun it describes, but its CASE from its job inside its own clause: Puella, quae puerum amat ("the girl who loves..." — quae is subject) vs. Rex, quem puella amat ("the king whom the girl loves" — quem is object). Masculine qui/quem, feminine quae/quam, neuter quod/quod.

drills.translation: The girl who loves the boy is good.
The boy who carries the water is good.
The war that we see is great.
The king whom the girl loves is good.
The city that the king sees is great.

points.title: The subjunctive mood: present and imperfect forms
points.function: Form the mood of wish, doubt, and dependent clauses

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The present subjunctive swaps the conjugation's vowel — first conjugation takes -e- (amem, ames, amet: "we shall see an -e- where amas has -a-"), the others take -a- (videat, dicat, audiat); sum gives sim, sis, sit. The imperfect subjunctive is the easiest form in Latin: infinitive + endings — amarem, videret, essem. On its own the subjunctive expresses wishes and exhortations: Vivat rex! ("Long live the king!"), Amemus! ("Let us love!"), utinam veniat ("if only she would come").

drills.translation: Let us praise the queen!
drills.hint: let us praise — hortatory present subjunctive

drills.translation: Long live the king!
drills.hint: may he live — present subjunctive wish

drills.translation: If only the girl would come!
drills.hint: may she come — present subjunctive after the wish word

drills.translation: If only I were in the city!
drills.hint: I were — imperfect subjunctive of sum

drills.translation: Let us hear the king's words!

points.title: Purpose clauses with ut and ne
points.function: Say why someone acts — in order to

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: Latin does not say "comes to see" with an infinitive: it uses ut + subjunctive — Puer venit ut puellam videat ("The boy comes so that he may see the girl"). Negative purpose takes ne: ne audiat ("so that he may not hear"). The tense follows the sequence rule: present subjunctive after a present main verb, imperfect subjunctive after a past one — dixit ut audiret.

drills.translation: The boy comes to see the girl.
drills.hint: may see — present subjunctive after ut

drills.translation: The king speaks so that the people may hear.
drills.hint: may hear — subjunctive in a purpose clause

drills.translation: The girl is silent so that the boy may not hear.
drills.hint: may hear — subjunctive after negative nē

drills.translation: The boy comes to carry the water.
drills.hint: may carry — first conjugation swaps its vowel to -e-

drills.translation: The king spoke so that the people might hear.
drills.hint: might hear — imperfect subjunctive after a past main verb

points.title: Result clauses: tam ... ut
points.function: Say that something is SO ... that ...

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: A signal word in the main clause — tam ("so"), tantus ("so great"), ita ("in such a way") — sets up ut + subjunctive for the outcome: Puella tam bona est ut puer eam amet ("The girl is so good that the boy loves her"). Unlike purpose clauses, a negative result keeps ut and adds non: ut non videat ("that he does not see").

drills.sentence: Puella tam bona est ut puer eam {{answer}}.
drills.translation: The girl is so good that the boy loves her.

drills.sentence: Bellum tam longum erat ut mīlitēs {{answer}}.
drills.translation: The war was so long that the soldiers fled.
drills.hint: fled — imperfect subjunctive in past result

drills.sentence: Rēx tam fortis est ut urbem {{answer}}.
drills.translation: The king is so brave that he captures the city.

drills.sentence: Puer tam celeriter currit ut puella eum nōn {{answer}}.
drills.translation: The boy runs so quickly that the girl does not see him.
drills.hint: sees — result clauses keep ut with nōn

drills.sentence: Tanta erat urbs ut omnēs eam {{answer}}.
drills.translation: So great was the city that everyone praised it.
drills.hint: praised — imperfect subjunctive in a past result clause

points.title: Cum-clauses: when, since, although
points.function: Read the three faces of cum + subjunctive

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: With the subjunctive, cum covers three ideas the context sorts out: circumstantial "when" (cum rex diceret — "when the king was speaking"), causal "since" (cum urbs magna sit — "since the city is great"), and concessive "although," usually flagged by tamen ("nevertheless") in the main clause. Past cum-clauses take the imperfect subjunctive for same-time action and the pluperfect for prior action: cum venisset — "when she had come."

drills.translation: When the king was speaking, the people were silent.
drills.hint: was speaking — imperfect subjunctive after cum

drills.translation: When the girl had come, the boy was happy.

drills.sentence: Cum urbs magna {{answer}}, multī eam vident.
drills.translation: Since the city is great, many people see it.
drills.hint: is — causal cum takes the subjunctive of esse

drills.sentence: Cum milites fortiter {{answer}}, urbs tamen capta est.
drills.translation: Although the soldiers fought bravely, the city was nevertheless captured.
drills.hint: were fighting — concessive cum, flagged by tamen

drills.sentence: Cum aquam nōn {{answer}}, puer trīstis erat.
drills.translation: Since he had no water, the boy was sad.

points.title: Indirect statement: accusative + infinitive
points.function: Report what someone says, knows, or thinks

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: After verbs of saying, knowing, and thinking, Latin drops "that" entirely: the reported subject goes into the ACCUSATIVE and the verb becomes an INFINITIVE. Dicit puellam cantare — literally "He says the girl to sing" = "He says that the girl is singing." The infinitive's tense is relative to the main verb: present cantare for same time, perfect portavisse for earlier time.

drills.translation: The boy says that the girl is singing.
drills.hint: to sing — present infinitive in reported speech

drills.translation: I know that the king is good.
drills.hint: to be — the infinitive that carries the reported claim

drills.translation: The girl says that the boy carried the water.
The king says that the soldiers are coming.
drills.hint: the soldiers — the reported subject goes accusative

drills.translation: I think that the girl is good.
drills.hint: good — agrees with the accusative subject

points.title: Ablative absolute
points.function: Fold background events into two ablative words

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: A noun and a participle, both in the ablative and grammatically detached from the rest of the sentence, set the scene: Urbe capta, milites venerunt ("With the city captured / after the city was captured, the soldiers came"). A perfect participle marks prior action (verbis dictis — "the words having been said"); a present participle marks simultaneous action (rege dicente — "while the king is speaking").

drills.translation: With the city captured, the soldiers came.
drills.hint: captured — ablative participle agreeing with the city

drills.translation: While the king is speaking, the people are silent.
drills.hint: speaking — present participle in the ablative

drills.translation: With the water carried, the boy comes.
drills.hint: the water — the ablative noun of the absolute phrase

drills.translation: With the war finished, we were happy.
drills.hint: finished — perfect participle in the ablative

drills.translation: With the words said, the king fell silent.

points.title: Deponent verbs: loquor, sequor
points.function: Passive endings, active meaning

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin conjugation
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: Deponent verbs "laid aside" their active forms: they wear passive endings but mean something active. Loquor = "I speak" (not "I am spoken"), sequor = "I follow," conor = "I try." Conjugate them exactly like passives — loquitur ("she speaks"), sequuntur ("they follow"), loquimur ("we speak") — and translate them actively, always.

drills.translation: The girl speaks with the boy.
The soldiers follow the king.
The boy tries to carry the water.
We speak in the city.
I follow you.

points.title: Gerund, gerundive, and the passive periphrastic
points.function: Handle Latin's verbal noun and the 'must be done' construction

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: The gerund is the verb's noun form (-ndum): ars amandi — "the art of loving." The gerundive is its adjective twin (-ndus, -a, -um), and with sum it forms the passive periphrastic of obligation: Carthago delenda est — "Carthage must be destroyed," Cato's famous refrain. The person who must act goes in the dative: nobis — "by us."

drills.translation: Carthage must be destroyed.
drills.hint: must be destroyed — the famous gerundive of obligation

drills.translation: The water must be carried.
drills.hint: must be carried — feminine gerundive + est

drills.translation: The art of loving is difficult.
The boy is eager to see.
drills.hint: of seeing — gerund after an adjective that takes the genitive

drills.translation: The king's words must be heard.
drills.hint: must be heard — neuter plural gerundive

points.title: Indirect questions and the sequence of tenses
points.function: Fold a question into another sentence

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: A question inside another verb — scio quid dicat, "I know what she is saying" — takes the SUBJUNCTIVE, and its tense obeys the sequence of tenses. After a primary (present/future) main verb: present subjunctive for same time (dicat), perfect for earlier (dixerit). After a secondary (past) main verb: imperfect for same time (diceret), pluperfect for earlier (cepisset).

drills.translation: I know what the girl is saying.
drills.hint: is saying — present subjunctive after a primary main verb

drills.translation: I ask who is carrying the water.
drills.hint: is carrying — subjunctive in an indirect question

drills.translation: I knew what the king was saying.
drills.hint: was saying — imperfect subjunctive after a past main verb

drills.translation: I know what the boy said.
drills.hint: said — perfect subjunctive for a prior action

drills.translation: I asked who had captured the city.
drills.hint: had captured — pluperfect subjunctive, past before past

points.title: Conditionals: the three types of si-clause
points.function: Distinguish real, should-would, and contrary-to-fact conditions

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: Open conditions take the indicative: si venit, laetus sum ("if she comes, I am happy"). Future-less-vivid ("should ... would") takes the present subjunctive in both halves: si veniat, laetus sim. Contrary-to-fact conditions use the imperfect subjunctive for the present (si veniret, laetus essem — "if she were coming, I would be happy") and the pluperfect for the past (si venisset, laetus fuissem — "if she had come, I would have been happy").

drills.translation: If the girl comes, I am happy.
drills.hint: comes — plain indicative for a real condition

drills.translation: If the girl should come, I would be happy.
drills.hint: should come — present subjunctive, the should-would type

drills.translation: If the girl were coming, I would be happy.
drills.hint: were coming — imperfect subjunctive, contrary to fact now

drills.translation: If the girl had come, I would have been happy.
drills.hint: had come — pluperfect subjunctive, contrary to fact in the past

drills.translation: If I had water, I would give it to you.
drills.hint: I had — imperfect subjunctive in a present contrary-to-fact

points.title: Oratio obliqua: sustained indirect discourse
points.function: Read whole reported speeches the way Caesar wrote them

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: Roman historians report entire speeches without quotation marks. In sustained oratio obliqua every main statement becomes accusative + infinitive, every subordinate clause slips into the subjunctive, and the speaker refers to himself with the reflexive se: Dixit se urbem cepisse — "He said that he (himself) had captured the city." Reported futures use the future participle: se portaturum (esse) — "that he would carry."

drills.translation: Caesar said that the soldiers had fought bravely.
drills.hint: to have fought — perfect infinitive in reported discourse

drills.sentence: Dīxit rēgem, quī urbem {{answer}}, bonum esse.
drills.translation: He said that the king, who held the city, was good.
drills.hint: held — subordinate clauses inside reported speech go subjunctive

drills.translation: He said that he would carry the water.
drills.hint: about to carry — future participle for a reported future

drills.translation: The king said that he had captured the city.
drills.hint: to have captured — perfect infinitive of capere

drills.translation: Caesar said that the enemy had been defeated.
drills.hint: defeated — perfect passive infinitive, participle + esse

points.title: Poetic word order: reading real classical lines
points.function: Untangle hyperbaton in verses every Roman knew

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: Poets pull agreeing words apart (hyperbaton) and trust the endings to reunite them: in Vergil's opening, Troiae ... ab oris wraps the relative clause, and the meaning waits until the case endings click together. Reading verse means holding endings in memory until their partners arrive — the discipline the whole case system has been training. These drills use genuine lines: Vergil, Horace, Catullus, and Caesar's famous prose opening.

drills.sentence: Arma virumque {{answer}}, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs.
drills.translation: Arms and the man I sing, who first from the shores of Troy... (Vergil, Aeneid 1.1)
drills.hint: I sing — the epic's opening main verb

drills.translation: Seize the day, trusting as little as possible in tomorrow. (Horace, Odes 1.11)

drills.sentence: Ōdī et {{answer}}. Quārē id faciam, fortasse requīris.
drills.translation: I hate and I love. Why do I do it, perhaps you ask. (Catullus 85)
drills.hint: I love — 1st person present, the second verb of the line

drills.sentence: Gallia est omnis dīvīsa in {{answer}} trēs.
drills.translation: All Gaul is divided into three parts. (Caesar, Gallic War 1.1)

drills.sentence: Tītyre, tū patulae recubāns sub tegmine {{answer}}.
drills.translation: Tityrus, you, reclining under the cover of a spreading beech... (Vergil, Eclogues 1.1)
drills.hint: of the beech tree — genitive singular

points.title: Register: Ciceronian period and colloquial Latin
points.function: Hear the difference between the speech and the letter

references.title: Wikipedia: Latin syntax
Allen & Greenough's New Latin Grammar (Dickinson College Commentaries)

points.explanation: High oratory builds the period — a long, suspended sentence whose sense completes only at the final verb — and reaches for figures like the accusative of exclamation (O tempora, o mores!). Letters and comedy talk instead: short questions (Quid agis? — "How are you?"), fixed formulas (salutem dicit — "sends greetings"; si vales, bene est, ego valeo). Both registers are correct Latin; a master reader switches between them.

drills.translation: How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience? (Cicero, In Catilinam 1)
drills.hint: our patience — ablative, because ūtī-compounds govern the ablative

drills.translation: O the times, o the customs! (Cicero)
drills.hint: the times — accusative of exclamation, neuter plural

drills.translation: How are you? (literally: what are you doing?) — the everyday colloquial greeting
drills.hint: you are doing — 2nd singular of agere

drills.translation: Cicero sends greetings to his dear Atticus. (the standard letter opening)
If you are well, it is good; I am well. (the stock letter formula)
drills.hint: I am well — 1st singular of the health verb
